questions.q: Who is this presentation actually for, and why does that change how it's built?
options: Azure support staff, for a technical review
The scheduling system vendor
Other DBAs, so it should focus on Bicep syntax details
Overlook's board — the same audience from Lesson 1 — who wants a direct, business-terms answer to whether a breach like the competitor's could happen here, not technical implementation details
questions.explain: The board wants the business translation of the work, not a tour of resource blocks and decorators.

questions.q: Why does the presentation specifically emphasize that the DR drill was unannounced?
options: Because that detail is what makes the proof credible rather than staged — the board can trust numbers from a test nobody scheduled or rehearsed
Because announced drills always produce better numbers
Because unannounced drills are required by Azure
It doesn't matter whether the drill was announced or not
questions.explain: An unannounced result carries real credibility that a scheduled, expected test result would not.

questions.q: What is the one honest trade-off this lesson says should be named plainly in the presentation?
options: That the board's mandate was unreasonable
That the failover group doesn't actually work
That TDE was never actually enabled
The readable secondary database's ongoing cost, stated plainly as the price of the RTO/RPO numbers being shown, not hidden in a later budget line
questions.explain: Naming this real cost openly, alongside its added reporting benefit, builds credibility rather than hiding it.

questions.q: Which sentence does this lesson hold up as the right way to talk about what the investment bought, versus the wrong way?
options: Only cost figures should be mentioned, with no mention of RTO/RPO
"We deployed a Bicep template with a failover group" is the right way to phrase it
"Overlook can now lose at most 44 seconds of data and be back up in under 20 minutes, proven in an unannounced test" is the right translation — a list of Azure resources is not
Neither sentence matters as long as the slides look professional
questions.explain: The board needs the outcome translated into something they can act on, not a list of resource types.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about presenting the project with zero caveats or trade-offs mentioned?
options: Trade-offs are irrelevant to a board presentation
It reads as either incomplete or dishonest to a board sophisticated enough to have asked these questions in the first place
Caveats should only be shared privately after the meeting
That's the ideal way to present to a board
questions.explain: An honest, complete account — including real costs — is what actually builds the credibility the original mandate was seeking.
